chunks: Going up in frequency makes the ripple smaller, because each cycle the inductor only has a short time to ramp, so the current ripple scales as one over f sw .
That means I can use a smaller inductor and smaller capacitors for the same ripple, and the control loop can be faster because I can push the crossover higher.
The price is efficiency and heat.

Every cycle I pay a fixed bit of energy: charging and discharging the gate, charging the switch-node capacitance, the overlap of voltage and current during the transitions, and the body-diode conduction in dead time.
Multiply by frequency and those losses scale linearly.
Core loss and EMI also get worse to deal with, and there's a hard ceiling from the minimum on-time: if I'm going from 12 volts to 1.
2 volts at 2 megahertz I need a 50 nanoseconds pulse, which a lot of controllers can't make. So the design is about finding the sweet spot. For a 12-to-3.
3 volts, 2 amps converter I'd probably choose something like 500 kilohertz to 1 megahertz.
Lower if I care about peak efficiency, higher if board area or transient response dominates."
